output.title: Standardised, timed cancer pathways with a fast-track referral
output.action: Adopt national cancer-specific pathways with maximum times per step and a single fast-track referral from primary care, following the Danish and Swedish model.
output.accountable_owner: Wellbeing services county, coordinated nationally by FICAN
output.mechanism: One referral criterion and booked slots replace sequential queues between primary care, imaging and the specialist clinic.

indicator_to_monitor.title: Patients waiting over 6 months during the year for access to specialised health care per 10 000 inhabitants

output.what_remains_unknown: Danish evidence is before/after without a control group. Patients left outside the pathway waited 4 days longer, so coverage must be monitored.

evidence.finding: After Denmark introduced standardised cancer patient pathways, the median diagnostic interval was 17 days shorter in 2010 than in 2004/05; patients not referred to a pathway waited 4 days longer.
evidence.unit: days, median diagnostic interval after vs before
evidence.citation: Jensen H, Tørring ML, Olesen F, Overgaard J, Fenger-Grøn M, Vedsted P. Diagnostic intervals before and after implementation of cancer patient pathways. BMC Cancer 2015;15:308.
evidence.caveat: Before/after without control group; two-tier risk for patients outside the pathway.

evidence.finding: Danish patients referred through a cancer patient pathway had a 1-year excess hazard ratio of 0.86 (0.73-1.01) vs patients not referred; 3-year relative survival rose from 45% to 54% across the implementation period.
evidence.unit: 1-year excess hazard ratio, pathway-referred vs not
evidence.citation: Jensen H, Tørring ML, Vedsted P. Prognostic consequences of implementing cancer patient pathways in Denmark. BMC Cancer 2017;17:627.
evidence.caveat: Interval includes 1; lead-time and secular-trend bias acknowledged by authors.

evidence.finding: Currently no unified national system guides disease-specific care guidelines or the implementation and monitoring of care pathways; existing guidelines, pathways, targets and indicators are not coordinated nationally, which perpetuates regional inequalities in access to and effectiveness of cancer care.

output.title: The same fast lane in public primary care that occupational care already gives
output.action: Same-week physician assessment and direct-access diagnostics for red-flag symptoms in public health centres, regardless of employment or insurance.
output.mechanism: In the Finnish DLBCL cohort the public route took a mean 207 days from symptom to treatment against 123 days through private or occupational care; most of the difference arises before the specialist visit.

indicator_to_monitor.title: Waiting time for elective outpatient medical visit (physician) in primary health care exceeds 7 days from assessment of the need for treatment, % appointments kept

output.what_remains_unknown: The route gap is observational and from one cancer type. How much of it a fast lane closes is a scenario parameter, not a measured effect.

evidence.finding: Finnish DLBCL cohort (n=160): mean cumulative days from symptom onset via private/occupational vs public primary care: first contact 42 vs 72, physician visit 43 vs 94, referral 77 vs 147, specialist visit 118 vs 204, treatment start 123 vs 207.
evidence.unit: days (mean symptom-to-treatment, public primary care minus private/occupational: 207 vs 123)
evidence.citation: Kuitunen H, et al. Socioeconomic Status and Access to Treatment in Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma. Cancer Med 2026;15(5):e71920, Figure 1.
evidence.caveat: Single cancer type, n=39 vs n=48, observational. Used as a labelled transferable prior for the shape of the route gap, not as a measured value for other cancers.

evidence.finding: Median symptom-to-treatment interval was 76 days via private/occupational care and 127 days via public primary care appointments.
evidence.unit: days (median symptom-to-treatment, 127 public vs 76 private/occupational; p=0.027)
evidence.citation: Kuitunen H, et al. Cancer Med 2026;15(5):e71920.

evidence.finding: In Finnish DLBCL, a symptom-to-biopsy interval over 7 weeks was associated with lower 2-year progression-free survival (74% vs 89%).
evidence.citation: Tokola S, et al. Cancer Med 2025;14(22):e71409.
evidence.caveat: Observational; no hazard ratio in the abstract.

output.title: Patient navigators for people whose work-up has stalled
output.action: A named nurse navigator contacts every patient whose suspected-cancer work-up passes 90 days without a diagnosis, and books the missing step.
output.mechanism: Targets the long tail of the pathway, where patients with fewer resources are over-represented.

indicator_to_monitor.title: Waiting time of over 3 months since assessment of the need for treatment for a non-emergency appointment with a primary health care doctor in outpatient care, % of completed appointments

output.what_remains_unknown: Trial evidence is from the United States; transfer to Finnish primary care is untested.

evidence.finding: Patient navigation increased the rate of diagnostic resolution after 90 days (adjusted HR 1.51) and of treatment start (HR 1.43).
evidence.unit: hazard ratio of diagnostic resolution, navigated vs usual care (days 91-365)
evidence.citation: Freund KM, et al. Impact of patient navigation on timely cancer care: the Patient Navigation Research Program. J Natl Cancer Inst 2014;106(6):dju115.
evidence.caveat: US safety-net populations; effect seen for patients already delayed beyond 90 days.

evidence.finding: In 469,522 Finnish cancer patients (2000-2019), lower education was associated with higher odds of stage IV disease at diagnosis.
evidence.unit: odds ratio of stage IV at diagnosis, lower vs higher education (women; men 1.10, 1.08-1.12)
evidence.citation: Zai X, Li P, Dei Bardi L, et al. Disparities in cancer incidence, stage at diagnosis, treatment and mortality across socioeconomic groups in Finland. BMJ Public Health 2025;3(2):e002829.

output.title: Targeted low-dose CT lung screening pilot
output.action: Invite current and former heavy smokers aged 50-74 to low-dose CT screening, starting where age-standardised lung cancer mortality is highest.
output.accountable_owner: Wellbeing services county with the national screening steering group
output.mechanism: Finnish five-year lung cancer survival is far below Sweden and Norway; screening shifts diagnoses to operable stages.
output.what_remains_unknown: Benefit accrues over about ten years and only in the screened group. Reach in Finland is an assumption.

evidence.finding: In the NELSON trial, volume CT screening of current and former heavy smokers reduced 10-year lung-cancer mortality in men (rate ratio 0.76).
evidence.citation: de Koning HJ, et al. Reduced lung-cancer mortality with volume CT screening in a randomized trial. N Engl J Med 2020;382:503-513.
evidence.caveat: Applies to the screened high-risk group only, not to all lung cancer deaths.

evidence.citation: Ministry of Social Affairs and Health / FICAN. National Cancer Strategy 2026-2035. Figure 1 and section 3.

output.title: HPV self-sampling kits for cervical screening non-attenders
output.action: Mail a self-sampling kit with the second reminder to everyone who has not attended.
output.mechanism: Removes the appointment, travel and language barriers for the people who do not come.

indicator_to_monitor.title: Proportion of women invited to cervical cancer screening (smear test) who attended, %

output.what_remains_unknown: The Finnish gain over a reminder letter is about 3 points, far smaller than the international pooled estimate.

evidence.finding: In Finland, reminder letters raised cervical screening participation from 72.6% to 79.2% and adding self-sampling raised it to 82.2%.
evidence.unit: percentage points (72.6% to 79.2% with reminder letters, 82.2% adding self-sampling)
evidence.citation: Virtanen A, et al. Improving cervical cancer screening attendance in Finland. Int J Cancer 2015;136(6):E677-E684.

evidence.finding: In a Finnish randomised trial among cervical screening non-attenders, a mailed HPV self-sampling kit gave relative participation 1.21 vs a reminder letter.
evidence.unit: relative participation, self-sampling kit vs reminder letter
evidence.citation: Virtanen A, et al. Self-sample HPV tests as an intervention for nonattendees of cervical cancer screening in Finland: a randomized trial. Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2011;20(9):1960-1969.

evidence.finding: Mailing HPV self-sampling kits to under-screened women gave pooled relative participation 2.33 vs invitation or reminder letters.
evidence.unit: relative participation, mailed kit vs letter (pooled RCTs)
evidence.citation: Arbyn M, et al. Detecting cervical precancer and reaching underscreened women by using HPV testing on self samples: updated meta-analyses. BMJ 2018;363:k4823.
evidence.caveat: International pooled estimate; the Finnish trial effect is much smaller and is the one used in the model.

output.what_remains_unknown: Interval cancers were non-inferior, not reduced: this is a capacity action, not a survival claim.

evidence.finding: In the MASAI randomised trial, AI-supported mammography reading reduced radiologist screen-reading workload by 44% with a cancer detection ratio of 1.29.

evidence.caveat: Interval-cancer result was non-inferior, not superior: supports capacity relief, not a survival claim.
